title: For each department, collect the distinct set of cities where its employees are based, producing a `Map<String, Set<String>>`, using `groupingBy` with a `mapping` downstream into `toSet`. Explain how nested collectors compose.
shortTitle: Collect the distinct set of cities per department using groupingBy with mapping to a Set
keyPoints: groupingBy(classifier, downstream) groups elements by a key and applies a downstream collector per group
mapping(mapper, downstream) transforms each element before it reaches the downstream collector
groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet())) yields Map<String, Set<String>>
toSet as the innermost collector collapses duplicate cities so each appears once per department
Collectors compose like building blocks: classifier picks the key, mapping picks the value, inner collector picks how to gather
Swapping toSet for toList keeps duplicates and order, so the innermost collector encodes the business rule
mapping on its own is rarely useful; it shines nested inside groupingBy or partitioningBy

s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, mapping(getCity, toSet()))` groups by department and keeps only the distinct cities per group.
s1_definition.profdef:
Nested collectors let one pass express a multi-level rule.

- **groupingBy(classifier, downstream)** – splits elements into groups by the classifier key and runs the downstream collector on each group's elements.
- **mapping(mapper, downstream)** – an adapting collector that applies the mapper to each element, then feeds the result into its own downstream collector.
- **toSet()** – gathers values into a `Set`, so duplicates collapse and each value appears once.
- **Composed together** – `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet()))` produces a `Map<String, Set<String>>` of distinct cities per department.
- **Building blocks** – each collector decides one thing: the key, the per-element value, or how values are gathered.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh sorts employee files into department trays at the National Bank of India. He does not want to keep whole files in each tray; he only wants the list of distinct cities. mapping pulls out just the city from each file as it drops into the tray, and the Set makes sure each city is listed once even if ten colleagues share it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
NESTED COLLECTORS COMPOSE AS BUILDING BLOCKS

          groupingBy( classifier , mapping( mapper , downstream ) )
                          │                 │             │
                          ▼                 ▼             ▼
                   pick the KEY       pick the VALUE   pick HOW to
                   (department)       (city)           GATHER (toSet)


FLOW FOR ONE GROUP (Trading)

  employees in Trading           mapping(getCity)         toSet()
 ┌───────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
 │ Rajesh  -> Mumbai      │────▶│ Mumbai         │────▶│              │
 │ Priya   -> Bangalore   │────▶│ Bangalore      │────▶│ {Mumbai,     │
 │ Amit    -> Mumbai      │────▶│ Mumbai         │────▶│  Bangalore}  │
 └───────────────────────┘     └────────────────┘     └──────────────┘
                                                        duplicate Mumbai
                                                        collapses to one


RESULT: Map<String, Set<String>>
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Trading  -> { Mumbai, Bangalore }          │
 │ Risk     -> { Delhi }                       │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

   swap toSet -> toList  ==>  Trading -> [Mumbai, Bangalore, Mumbai]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The mapping collector transforms each element before it reaches a downstream collector, and it becomes powerful when nested inside groupingBy. By writing groupingBy of department with a downstream of mapping of city into toSet, you group employees by department and, within each group, keep only the distinct cities rather than the whole employee objects. The toSet collapses duplicate cities so each appears once per department.

In our work at the National Bank of India, Rajesh planned regional training and needed, for each department, the unique set of cities where its staff were based so the bank could book venues. If two Trading colleagues were both in Mumbai he did not want Mumbai listed twice, and the mapping-into-Set downstream gave him exactly the distinct cities per department in a single collect call.

The point to always make is that collectors compose like building blocks, and each block expresses one part of the business rule. The classifier chooses the key, mapping chooses what value each element contributes, and the innermost collector chooses how the values are gathered: toSet for distinctness, toList to keep duplicates and order, counting for a tally, joining for a string. Changing just the innermost collector changes the business meaning without touching the grouping logic.

When you also need sorted output, the three-argument groupingBy lets you pick a TreeMap for the keys and a toCollection of TreeSet for the values, so both the departments and the cities come out in order. That same compose-the-blocks thinking scales from a two-level rule to deeper ones.

Remember one sentence: the classifier picks the key, mapping picks the value, and the innermost collector picks how to gather, so distinct-cities-per-department is just groupingBy plus mapping plus toSet.
